title: Insertion sort
short: Sort like a hand of cards: slide each new one into place.
what: Keep the left part of the list sorted. Take the next item and slide it left past every bigger item until it fits. Repeat until the whole list is the sorted part.
analogy: Picking up playing cards one at a time. Each new card goes into your hand right where it belongs, and the cards to its right shuffle over to make room.

frames.label: insertion sort
frames.say: Like a hand of cards: 5 alone is a sorted hand. Pick up the next card, 2.

frames.label: insertion sort
frames.say: 2 is smaller than 5, so they swap. The sorted part is now 2, 5.

frames.label: insertion sort
frames.say: Pick up 4. It is smaller than 5, so it swaps once, then stops because 2 is smaller.

frames.label: insertion sort
frames.say: Pick up 6. It is bigger than 5, so it stays put. Zero moves: this is why nearly sorted input is fast.

frames.label: insertion sort
frames.say: Pick up 1. It is smaller than everything, so it slides past 6, 5, 4 and 2. Four moves: the slow case.

frames.label: insertion sort
frames.say: Pick up 3. It slides past 6, 5 and 4, and stops next to 2.

frames.label: insertion sort
frames.say: Sorted. 9 moves in total: one for each pair that started in the wrong order. Reversed input is the worst.

when: The list is small (a few dozen items)
The list is almost sorted already
Items arrive one at a time and must stay sorted
You must sort in place with O(1) extra memory
python:
def insertion_sort(a):
    moves = 0
    for i in range(1, len(a)):
        j = i
        while j > 0 and a[j - 1] > a[j]:
            a[j - 1], a[j] = a[j], a[j - 1]
            j -= 1
            moves += 1
    return moves

nums = [5, 2, 4, 6, 1, 3]
print(insertion_sort(nums), nums)
watch: Use a[j - 1] > a[j], not >=, so equal items keep their order (stable).
It is O(n²) on random data. Above a few dozen items, use sorted().
To keep a list sorted as items arrive, bisect.insort does this for you.
